topic: Antimicrobial Stewardship Principles — The Five Ds
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Antimicrobial Stewardship Programme
speakerBio: Clinical lead for the hospital's antimicrobial stewardship programme; spends her days at the interface of the microbiology bench and the ward round, and believes the best antibiotic is often the one you stop.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

It is 2 a.m. on the medical admissions unit. A 74-year-old with a productive cough, a temperature of 38.4°C and a mild AKI is written up for piperacillin–tazobactam plus a stat dose of meropenem "to be safe" by a tired SHO. Nobody sent a sputum. Nobody wrote a stop date. Nobody will review it at 48 hours because the patient is being moved to a base ward. This is how resistance is made — not by one reckless prescriber, but by a thousand small, defensible-in-the-moment decisions. This session is about the discipline that undoes that: antimicrobial stewardship.

1 · Why stewardship matters — the tragedy of the commons 🌍

Every antibiotic dose is a decision that affects two patients: the one in front of you, and every future patient who will be infected by the organisms you help select. The antibiotic works on the individual; the resistance it selects is shared by the whole ward, the whole hospital, the whole community. This is a textbook tragedy of the commons: each prescriber, acting rationally to protect their own patient, degrades a resource — antibiotic effectiveness — that belongs to everyone.

Antibiotics are the only class of drug where use in one patient reduces the effectiveness of the drug in every other patient. You are prescribing from a shared, non-renewable account.

The scale is not abstract. Drug-resistant infections are associated with well over a million deaths worldwide each year and are projected to become one of the leading causes of death by mid-century if trends continue. Meanwhile the discovery pipeline has largely dried up — we are spending a resource we cannot easily replace.

2 · The four harms of getting it wrong ☠️

HarmMechanismWhy it bites
Resistance selectionAntibiotic kills susceptible flora and leaves resistant mutants to expand unopposedThe next infection in this patient — and this ward — is harder to treat
Collateral damageBroad-spectrum agents wipe the protective commensal microbiome (gut, skin, mucosa)Colonisation resistance is lost → overgrowth of C. difficile, Candida, resistant Gram-negatives
Clostridioides difficileDisruption of colonic flora, classically by fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclavToxin-mediated colitis; can be fatal; drives isolation, ward closures, cost
Direct drug toxicityAKI, C. diff, rash, anaphylaxis, QT prolongation, cytopenias, Clostridioides, candidaemiaAn antibiotic given "just in case" still carries all its downsides for no benefit
💡 One-liner

"Just in case" is not free. An unnecessary antibiotic can only harm — the patient without infection gets none of the benefit and all of the risk.

3 · The mechanism of resistance selection — drawn out step by step 🔬

Understand the vicious cycle and you will never over-prescribe casually again:

  1. A patient carries a mixed population of bacteria — mostly susceptible, a tiny minority carrying resistance genes (spontaneous mutants, or plasmid-borne genes acquired horizontally).
  2. You give a broad-spectrum antibiotic. It kills the susceptible majority, including the harmless commensals that were competing for space and nutrients.
  3. The resistant minority now faces no competition and no drug pressure it cannot survive → it expands to fill the vacated niche (selective amplification).
  4. Those resistant organisms shed into the environment, transfer plasmids to neighbours (horizontal gene transfer), and colonise the next patient via hands, equipment and surfaces.
  5. The longer and broader the exposure, the more complete the selection. Duration and spectrum are the two dials that turn the ratchet.

Crucially, resistance is often selected, not created, by antibiotics — the genes frequently pre-exist; the drug simply clears the field for them. That is why every unnecessary day and every unnecessary spectrum-widening matters.

4 · The Five Ds of stewardship 🖐️

The organising framework for optimal antimicrobial use. Get all five right and you protect both patients — the present one and the future one.

DPrincipleIn practice
Right DrugCorrect agent for the likely/known pathogen, with the narrowest adequate spectrum and best tissue penetrationEmpirically cover the likely bugs and local resistance patterns; the moment you can, narrow it
Right DosePK/PD-optimised dosing — enough to hit the target at the site of infection, adjusted for organ function and weightLoading doses in sepsis; watch augmented renal clearance; don't reflexively under-dose the sick (see Session 11)
De-escalationNarrow spectrum once cultures/sensitivities return; stop redundant coverPiperacillin–tazobactam → co-amoxiclav or a narrow agent once the organism is known (Session 10)
DurationThe shortest course supported by evidence — stop when the job is doneMost infections: 5–7 days, not 10–14; write a stop/review date on day 1 (Session 10)
De-escalation of route (IV→oral)Switch to oral as soon as the patient is improving and can absorb — removes line risk, frees the patientApply IV-to-oral switch criteria daily; many agents have excellent oral bioavailability
💡 Memory hook — the 5 Ds

Drug, Dose, De-escalation (of spectrum), Duration, De-escalation of route. Right bug-drug, right amount, narrow it, stop it, swallow it.

Start smart, then focus. Broad and early to save the septic patient; narrow and short to save everyone else.

5 · Broad-spectrum overuse — the ecological cost 🌱

Broad-spectrum agents are not "stronger" — they are wider. Width is precisely the problem for the ecosystem:

  • Carbapenems select for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) and are the last-line for ESBLs — every unnecessary meropenem erodes the reserve.
  • Fluoroquinolones and 3rd-gen cephalosporins are among the strongest drivers of C. difficile and of ESBL selection.
  • Anti-pseudomonal β-lactams (piperacillin–tazobactam, ceftazidime) select for AmpC de-repression and Pseudomonas resistance.

The "collateral damage" concept: the wider the spectrum, the more of the protective commensal flora you destroy, and the more ecological room you create for the very MDR organisms you fear. Broad empiric therapy is a loan against the future — justified in genuine sepsis, but it must be repaid promptly by de-escalation.

6 · What a stewardship programme actually does 🏛️

Stewardship is not one clever prescriber — it is a system. A core Antimicrobial Stewardship Programme (ASP) has physician and pharmacist leadership, IT/data support, microbiology, and infection-control partnership, with the backing of hospital leadership. Its two evidence-backed core strategies:

StrategyHow it worksTrade-off
Prospective audit & feedbackAn ASP pharmacist/physician reviews active prescriptions (e.g. at 48–72 h) and recommends narrowing, stopping or switching directly to the treating teamPreserves prescriber autonomy; labour-intensive; the preferred, best-evidenced approach
Formulary restriction & prior authorisationRestricted agents (carbapenems, last-line drugs) require approval from micro/ID before or shortly after usePowerful and immediate, but can delay therapy and shift use to unrestricted agents ("squeezing the balloon")

Supporting tactics: institutional guidelines and care bundles, an antibiogram (local cumulative susceptibility data) to guide empiric choices, automatic IV-to-oral switch protocols, dose-optimisation programmes, allergy de-labelling, rapid diagnostics, and mandatory documented indication + stop/review date at prescription.

🎯 The 48–72 hour "antibiotic time-out"

The single most useful stewardship habit for a ward team: at 48–72 hours, when cultures are back and the patient's trajectory is clear, actively ask — Do we still need an antibiotic? Can we narrow it? Can we switch to oral? When will we stop? Empiric therapy started in uncertainty must be revisited in the light of data.

7 · The prescriber's daily checklist 📋

  1. Is this actually infection? Fever and a raised CRP are not synonyms for bacterial infection — exclude mimics before reaching for a drug.
  2. Cultures before antibiotics (without delaying therapy in sepsis) — you cannot de-escalate what you never characterised.
  3. Narrowest adequate empiric agent guided by the local antibiogram and the source.
  4. Document indication and a stop/review date — every time.
  5. Review at 48–72 h: de-escalate, switch to oral, or stop.
☠️ M&M — the "safety-net" carbapenem that wasn't safe

A 68-year-old woman was admitted with a simple lower UTI. Her previous urine had grown an ESBL E. coli, so she was started on meropenem — reasonable. But the flag never came off: at 48 hours no one reviewed the sensitivities, which showed the organism was fully susceptible to oral nitrofurantoin. She stayed on IV meropenem for ten days through a long line. On day 7 she developed profuse diarrhoea — C. difficile colitis — progressing to toxic megacolon and a colectomy. Lesson: the failure was not the empiric choice; it was the absence of de-escalation. A UTI that could have been treated with a five-day oral tablet became a life-threatening iatrogenic illness because nobody applied the 4th and 5th Ds. Broad-and-early is only safe if it is followed by narrow-short-oral.

8 · Take-home 🎓

  • Two patients, every prescription: the one in front of you and every future patient who inherits the resistance you select.
  • The 5 Ds: right Drug, right Dose, De-escalation of spectrum, Duration (short), De-escalation of route (IV→oral).
  • Resistance is selected, not usually created — duration and spectrum are the two dials; turn them down whenever you safely can.
  • Broad-spectrum overuse has an ecological cost: C. difficile, collateral damage, CRE, candidaemia. A broad empiric loan must be repaid by de-escalation.
  • Stewardship is a system: prospective audit & feedback and formulary restriction, an antibiogram, and a mandatory 48–72 h time-out.
  • Do the ward-level thing: indication + stop date on day 1, and a genuine review at 48–72 hours.

moderatorQs.q: You describe antibiotics as prescribing from a 'shared account'. What does that change about how a clinician should think at the bedside?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It reframes every prescription as affecting two patients: the individual in front of you, who gets the benefit and the toxicity, and every future patient who inherits the resistant flora you help select. Antibiotics are unique in that use in one patient degrades effectiveness for everyone — a tragedy of the commons. Practically, it means an unnecessary antibiotic is never neutral: it can only harm (C. difficile, resistance, direct toxicity) with no offsetting benefit. So the bedside question shifts from 'could this be infection?' to 'is an antibiotic genuinely justified, and if so, what is the narrowest, shortest course that treats it?'

moderatorQs.q: Walk us through the mechanism by which a broad-spectrum antibiotic selects resistance — why does duration matter so much?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A patient carries a mixed flora — mostly susceptible organisms plus a tiny resistant minority whose genes usually pre-exist. A broad agent kills the susceptible majority and the protective commensals, removing both the competition and the drug-susceptible competitors. The resistant minority then expands unopposed into the vacated niche (selective amplification) and can transfer resistance plasmids horizontally to neighbours and colonise the next patient. Resistance is therefore usually selected, not created. Duration matters because every extra day of exposure prolongs the selective pressure that amplifies the resistant subpopulation — duration and spectrum are the two dials that turn the ratchet, which is exactly why 'shorter and narrower' is protective.

moderatorQs.q: Compare prospective audit and feedback with formulary restriction — which does a mature programme lean on, and why?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Both are core, evidence-based strategies. Prospective audit & feedback has an ASP pharmacist/physician review live prescriptions at 48–72 h and recommend narrowing, switching or stopping directly to the team — it preserves prescriber autonomy, educates in real time, and has the strongest evidence, so mature programmes lean on it. Formulary restriction / prior authorisation gates restricted agents (carbapenems, last-line drugs) behind micro/ID approval; it is powerful and immediate but can delay therapy and simply shift usage to unrestricted agents ('squeezing the balloon'). Most programmes use restriction for the truly last-line agents and audit-and-feedback for everything else.

audienceQs.q: On a busy take, what is the single most useful stewardship habit I can actually do myself?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Two things, both quick. First, at prescription, document the indication and a stop/review date — never write an antibiotic without a plan to stop it. Second, at 48–72 hours do an 'antibiotic time-out': cultures are back and the trajectory is clear, so actively ask do we still need it, can we narrow it, can we switch to oral, when do we stop? Most inappropriate antibiotic-days come not from a bad empiric choice but from nobody revisiting it. You don't need to be an ID specialist to de-escalate — you just need to look.

audienceQs.q: How do I convince a reluctant team to de-escalate from piperacillin–tazobactam when the patient is clinically better?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Anchor it in the data on the chart, not opinion. Show the culture and sensitivities: if the organism is susceptible to a narrower agent, de-escalation is the guideline-concordant move and there is no evidence that staying broad improves outcomes in a responding patient. Frame the harms concretely — continued pip-tazudrives AmpC selection and, with the long line, C. difficile and line infection risk. Offer a specific alternative and an IV-to-oral switch if criteria are met, and put a stop date on it. Teams de-escalate readily when you bring the sensitivity report and a concrete narrower plan rather than a general principle.

audienceQs.q: Doesn't stewardship conflict with Surviving Sepsis — which tells me to give broad antibiotics fast?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — they are two halves of the same discipline. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 rightly demands early, broad, adequately-dosed empiric therapy for the septic patient, because inadequate initial cover costs lives. Stewardship governs what happens next: 'start smart, then focus'. The broad empiric choice is a justified loan against the future, but it must be repaid by de-escalation once cultures return, an IV-to-oral switch when the patient stabilises, and the shortest evidence-based duration. Broad-and-early and narrow-short-later are complementary, not contradictory — the error is taking the loan and never repaying it.
